title: Thinking Machines Unveils Inkling 2 Mini, A Powerful 26B Parameter AI Model That Runs Locally On MacBooks With Just 32GB RAM
summary: Thinking Machines unveils Inkling 2 Mini, a 26B parameter AI model for MacBooks
detailed: Thinking Machines Lab launched Inkling 2 Mini, a 26-billion-parameter open-weight AI model that runs locally on consumer hardware with 32GB of RAM.
The model uses a 24-layer Mixture of Experts architecture where middle layers execute multiple times, yielding an effective active count of 5.4 billion parameters per token.
Inkling 2 Mini achieved an Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score of 20.1 and scored 77.9% on SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard.
The model was trained using NVIDIA's GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra platform with 4-bit NVFP4 and 8-bit MXFP8 precisions to avoid quantization losses.
This development matters because it enables developers to run powerful reasoning and coding agents locally on edge devices like Apple MacBooks without cloud infrastructure.
sentences: Thinking Machines Lab has unveiled Inkling 2 Mini, a surprisingly capable new open-weight AI model that packs just 26 billion parameters while delivering impressive performance in coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads.
More importantly, t he model can run entirely offline on consumer hardware, including Apple MacBooks equipped with 32GB of unified memory.
Announced on November 20, Inkling 2 Mini arrives as a considerably smaller alternative to the company's massive 594-billion-parameter Inkling 2 Small.

However, rather than simply shrinking an existing architecture, Thinking Machines has adopted an interesting approach that allows its new model to perform additional reasoning without generating more tokens.
The results are promising, with the model achieving an Artificial Analysis (AA) Intelligence Index score of 20.1, alongside competitive performance against considerably larger AI models.

According to Thinking Machines' official technical announcement, Inkling 2 Mini uses a 24-layer Mixture of Experts (MoE) transformer architecture, with 26.4 billion total parameters and just 3.4 billion active parameters.
What makes this architecture particularly interesting is how it processes information.
Rather than passing every token through each transformer layer just once, the model executes its middle 12 layers three times, while the first and last six layers operate normally.
Consequently, the model performs 48 layer applications per token despite storing the weights for only 24 layers.
This increases its effective active parameter count to 5.4 billion per token, allowing additional computation without proportionally increasing its memory requirements.
In simpler terms, Inkling 2 Mini can effectively spend more time reasoning internally before producing its next token.
The company claims this approach delivers particularly impressive improvements in agentic coding.
Inkling 2 Mini achieved 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, compared with 42.2% for Qwen3.8-27B, while its SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard score reached 77.9%, surpassing the latter's 73.8%.
It also scored 46.5% on the Vals Index v2.2 and 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified.
These are company-reported evaluation results, and differences in testing configurations mean they shouldn't be interpreted as universal performance advantages.
Interestingly, Thinking Machines trained Inkling 2 Mini on NVIDIA's GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra platform, leveraging its hardware-accelerated NVFP4 capabilities to improve training efficiency.
Most of the model's weights were trained using 4-bit NVFP4 precision, with the final four layers employing 8-bit MXFP8 precision.
Since these weights are deployed in the same numerical precision used during training, the company says the model avoids additional conversion losses associated with post-training quantization.
Perhaps the most exciting aspect of Inkling 2 Mini is its accessibility.
Despite its capabilities, the model has a memory footprint of approximately 20GB, allowing it to run on Apple silicon Macs with at least 32GB of unified memory through Ollama.
NVIDIA's DGX Spark desktop AI computer is also officially supported, while other GPU configurations are possible, with 32GB or more of VRAM recommended.
The model supports text and image inputs, alongside a context window extending up to one million tokens.
To demonstrate its capabilities, Thinking Machines showcased Inkling 2 Mini running completely offline on an M5 Pro MacBook Pro equipped with 48GB of memory.
During a flight, the model reportedly generated a playable flight simulator in just a few minutes.
However, the architecture introduces an important question concerning AI safety and transparency.

Because looped transformers can perform additional computation internally without explicitly writing down every reasoning step, researchers have raised concerns about whether their behavior becomes more difficult to monitor.

Thinking Machines investigated this using a separate variable-loop research model, discovering that additional passes increased the model's ability to solve problems without producing a written chain of thought.
Its measured no-chain-of-thought task horizon increased from 16 seconds with one pass to 37 seconds with three.
Nevertheless, the company's experiments found that the model's written reasoning remained understandable, without a meaningful reduction in monitorability at this scale.
The researchers also acknowledged limitations, including weaker performance on complex multi-turn conversations and instructions involving numerous constraints.

Inkling 2 Mini is now available under the Apache 2.0 license, with downloadable weights on Hugging Face, local deployment through Ollama, and inference and fine-tuning through Thinking Machines' Tinker platform.

For developers interested in running capable AI agents locally rather than relying exclusively on cloud infrastructure, Inkling 2 Mini represents another interesting development in making advanced AI models more accessible.
